title: Adoro te devote
hook: Hopkins translated it: Godhead here in hiding, whom I do adore

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Corpus Christi hymns: Pange lingua, and its last verses, the Tantum ergo. Your line was sing, my tongue. What did you say or sing aloud? Day one thousand one hundred eighty-one.

A poet sits with a Latin hymn and tries to carry it over into English without spilling any. The poet is Gerard Manley Hopkins, a Jesuit priest whose own poems bend English into strange new music. The hymn is one tradition credits to Thomas Aquinas, a quiet prayer before the Eucharist. Its first words are Adoro te devote: I adore you devoutly. And Hopkins's English opens with a line that turns a doctrine into a picture: Godhead here in hiding, whom I do adore. Yesterday's hymns were for processions and choirs. This one is for one person, kneeling.
screen: `A POET AND A LATIN HYMN.` → `ADORO TE DEVOTE.` → `GODHEAD HERE IN HIDING.`

segments.voice: Here's the Latin opening: "Adoro te devote, latens Deitas." I adore you devoutly, hidden Godhead. Latens means lying hidden. The hymn is built on that one idea: God present, but out of sight. It isn't a new idea in scripture. Isaiah, in the Douay-Rheims, says: "Verily thou art a hidden God, the God of Israel the saviour." Then the second verse goes straight at the senses: "Visus, tactus, gustus in te fallitur." Sight, touch and taste are deceived in you. And here's a wrinkle. Two days ago, in the Summa, Thomas was careful to say the senses are not deceived at Mass, because the appearances of bread really are there. The hymn speaks from the pew: the eyes see bread, the tongue tastes bread, and they can't reach what's underneath. Some readers put it this way: one is explaining; the other is kneeling. So what's left to trust? The hymn answers: hearing. "Sed auditu solo tuto creditur." Only by hearing is it safely believed. Hearing what? The word of Christ, who said this is my body. Paul says it in Romans: "Faith then cometh by hearing; and hearing by the word of Christ." The hymn then says, in effect, I believe whatever the Son of God has said, for nothing is truer than Truth's own word. That's the whole movement of the prayer: the eyes come up empty, the ears catch a word, and the heart bows. Scholars have debated whether Thomas wrote this hymn himself; tradition keeps his name on it. Either way, it sounds like someone who spent his life thinking about what can't be seen.
screen: `LATENS DEITAS: HIDDEN GODHEAD.` · `SIGHT, TOUCH, TASTE ARE DECEIVED.` · `ONLY BY HEARING.` · `EXPLAINING AND KNEELING.` · then, large: `VERILY THOU ART A HIDDEN GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray the first verse. Settle, and breathe. If you pray, say the first verse of this hymn slowly, in Latin if you know it, or in Hopkins's English, which begins with today's line. If you don't know it, just say the opening, Adoro te devote, latens Deitas, and let it sit. If you don't pray, take the line Godhead here in hiding and simply notice one thing near you that's real but can't be seen: love in a house, trust in a friendship, air in the room. The bell holds the time.
Adoro te devote. I adore you devoutly: the opening of a hymn to God hidden in the Eucharist, credited by tradition to Thomas, and carried into English by Hopkins. Today's word.
Your line: godhead here in hiding. Today, when your eyes say there's nothing there, listen for a word instead. Day one thousand one hundred eighty-one.

howItsDone: Catholics pray the Adoro te devote during Eucharistic adoration and before or after Communion, either in Latin or in English versions, including Hopkins's translation.

notes: Hopkins's line 'Godhead here in hiding, whom I do adore' is given in the voice without quotation marks and cited with quoted: null, because Hopkins is not on the validator's public-domain list. Hopkins died before 1900 and the poem was published posthumously in 1918, so it should be public domain; an editor may add quotation marks if Hopkins is added to the list.

Latin wording to confirm: Adoro te v. 1 opening and v. 2 lines 1–2. The paraphrase 'I believe whatever the Son of God has said; nothing is truer than Truth's own word' renders 'Credo quidquid dixit Dei Filius: nil hoc verbo Veritatis verius.'
Authorship: the voice says scholars have debated whether Thomas wrote it and tradition keeps his name on it; confirm the framing.

The tension between the hymn's 'fallitur' and ST III.75.5 ad 2 (the senses are not deceived about accidents) is presented as explaining vs praying, not contradiction; a Keeper may prefer a different reconciliation.
Douay-Rheims wording to confirm: Isaiah 45:15 and Romans 10:17.

Editor pass: 'fallitur' now rendered 'are deceived' (not 'fall short'), so the stated tension with ST III.75.5 ad 2 is visible; the reconciliation is attributed to 'some readers' instead of asserted by the narrator; removed a line telling the listener how the pew feels.
